title: Systems leadership, change, and convening
description: My writing and talks on systems leadership, systems change, and convening: recurring patterns, purpose, power, boundaries, and the capacity to act together.

groups.title: Start here
groups.description: My current definition and the two companion essays that set out the distinctions.

items.title: Where are the systems in ‘systems leadership’?
items.description: What I mean by systems leadership, how it differs from leadership and personal development, and why changing recurring patterns requires more than developing the people at the top. Includes my response to the public health paper shared by Greg Fell.

items.title: Systems leadership: make inquiry actionable
items.meta: 24 October 2026 · The Necessary Tangle · practice guide
items.description: Follow a recurring pattern to the rules, resources, and authority that maintain it. Distinguish a helpful exception from a changed arrangement, and keep inquiry inside the action.

items.title: Six ways to see systems leadership
items.meta: 22 June 2021 · Integration and Implementation Insights · article
items.description: Six overlapping approaches to systems leadership, with different implications for effectiveness, power, legitimacy, and change. The concise introduction to the framework.

items.title: A schema for better understanding systems leadership and systems change
items.meta: 21 June 2021 · Systems Community of Inquiry · companion essay
items.description: The fuller companion to ‘Six ways’, with examples, references, and the assumptions and risks of each approach, including individual development masquerading as leadership development.

items.title: A response to The Inner Work of System Leadership
items.meta: 18 March 2026 · Systems Community of Inquiry · response to Kania, Ruparell, Senge, and Hamilton
items.description: Questions the claim that inner work is a prerequisite for systems change, and argues for explicit attention to power, conflict, incentives, enforcement, and learning through action.

items.title: What can systems thinking and change learn to become?
items.meta: 2024 · appendix to Understanding Systems to Change the World · PDF
items.description: Eight pitfalls in systems thinking and change, from mistaking a model for reality to ignoring power and lived experience, with eight practical responses. Published in 2024; this extract was shared in 2026.

items.title: What is #systemschange exactly? Why and when do we need it?
items.description: Different meanings of systems change, and the importance of perspectives, boundaries, identities, rules, and power when deciding what needs to change.

items.title: What might systems leadership be? And how does it relate to systems change? A happily tentative essay
items.meta: 3 August 2020 · Systems Community of Inquiry · earlier essay
items.description: The exploratory essay that preceded the 2021 framework, surveying different meanings of leadership, change, and convening, with examples and further reading.

items.title: Lankelly Chase’s approach to working with complexity — with comments
items.meta: 4 June 2018 · Systems Community of Inquiry · commentary on Julian Corner’s article
items.description: My annotations question whether desirable behaviours explain systemic effectiveness, and examine the roles of structure, incentives, power, participation, and accountability.

items.title: An instant review of Whole-System Development: The Capacity to Act Together — Janoff (2026)
items.meta: 1 July 2026 · Systems Community of Inquiry · full review
items.description: How working with differences can develop the capacity for joint action, with questions about power, boundaries, and learning after the event.

links.title: A wise perspective on building the capacity to act together in ‘whole systems’
links.label: Read the shorter Chosen Path version

items.title: What if the most valuable thing in ‘whole system’ work is not seeing the whole system at all?
items.description: How bringing people together can expand understanding without revealing a complete, objective ‘whole system’. A later reflection connecting convening to the critical questions in my 2024 appendix.

items.title: Is ‘systems convening’ a thing?
items.meta: 15 September 2021, revised 16 September · Chosen Path · essay
items.description: A critical examination of systems convening as an observed practice: social learning, context, naming, recognition, and the risks of turning it into a formula.

items.title: Something new has been named: #systemsconvening
items.description: Why naming systems convening can recognise and support people already doing the work, and how codification and fashionable adoption can distort it.

items.title: Systems convening and boundary work
items.description: A compact route into systems convening and working across boundaries.

items.title: Spaces and leadership stands
items.description: Systemic position and possible leadership responses.

items.title: Systems Leadership, Systems Change, Systems Theory, and Systems Practice (And Systems Convening)
items.meta: 28 June 2023 · Open University systems community · presentation PDF
items.description: The later presentation bringing together systems leadership, change, theory, practice, and convening, with questions about legitimacy, effectiveness, and learning.

items.title: Systems Leadership, Change, Theory and Practice — SCiO
items.meta: 11 July 2022 · SCiO · recorded talk and presentation
items.description: The SCiO session developing the two 2021 articles, exploring the different meanings of systems leadership and systems change. SCiO’s resource page brings the recording and presentation together.

items.title: What the hell is systems | complexity | cybernetics anyway?
items.meta: 13 June 2022 · Chosen Path · introduction to the systems-convening community session
items.description: How systems thinking and practice can contribute to systems convening, through framing, boundaries, power, agency, and learning. The session, ‘Systems convening, systems thinking, and systems practice’, is available below.

items.title: The walls come back: why relational public services fail after they work
items.description: Why successful relational pilots remain fragile when funding, authority, measures, and accountability retain the previous arrangements, and what must change for the work to last.
